claim: A filter byte's corner sits on a single pole, and both filters this type's type byte selects are one pole each. The low pass falls six decibels an octave through the middle of the band and the high pass the same the other way; neither is a biquad and neither is two poles cascaded, which would be twelve. The low pass carries the zero the bilinear transform leaves at half the rate, and that is what makes a clock readable off it: the skirt bends from 5.7 decibels an octave between 800 Hz and 1.6 kHz to 10.3 between 6.4 and 12.7 kHz, which puts half the rate just above the top of the band and the rate at thirty-two kilohertz. Read at forty-four or forty-eight it is four times worse and leans. The high pass names the order and cannot name the rate: its corners are all under 500 Hz, its zero is at nothing, and the place a warp would show is its own flat passband. One corner table serves both -- at the four settings both were read the two agree to within 0.064 octaves, which is what this reading resolves.
named: a one-pole section, the same one written twice with its numerator changed

rows: Stereo Chorus, parameter 1, Pre Filter (Pre filter), Off, LPF, HPF, LPF+HPF
document_rows.why: That the byte at 40 03 03 chooses which filter runs and that its off state is one of the four the page prints, which is what the flat reference every profile here is read against was taken at. A page saying so is evidence about a page; what makes it a measurement is that the reference profile is flat.

era_priors.claim: A pole costs one stored coefficient and a pair costs two, so a part with a sixteen-entry corner table spends sixteen numbers on one pole and thirty-two on a pair.
era_priors.why: The frequency class argues a table of sixteen corners is affordable and a table of a hundred and twenty-eight is not, and what an entry holds is the quantity that argument is about. Measuring the order is therefore a test of the prior that class was carried by, and it came back on the cheap side of it.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: A skirt on any of this part's corner bytes ran at twelve decibels an octave. The prior is about what a stored entry can cost, and a pair measured anywhere would say the part pays it -- after which a sixteen-entry table is no longer the cheap reading it is being argued to be.

adds: The records say what the cutoff byte did to each twelfth-octave band at eleven settings as a low pass and four as a high pass, and each carries the steepest slope it was running at. What is read out of them here is that those slopes are one pole and not two, that the same is true on both filters, that one corner table serves the two, and that where the low pass's skirt stops behaving like an analogue one names the clock. The records name no filter, no corner and no order, and say so.

what_the_type_byte_is.what: A selector with an off state, and the off state is the absence of the section rather than the section pushed out of the way. The reference profile taken at it is flat to a tenth of a decibel across the whole band set, which a one-pole low pass parked at the top of its table would not be -- its zero at half the rate would still be cutting the top bands.
what_the_type_byte_is.against: the run's own flat repeats, which spread 0.04 to 0.14 dB above 100 Hz.

what_the_corner_table_is.what: One table, read by whichever filter the type byte switched in. At the four settings both filters were asked the corners agree to 0.027, 0.038, 0.064 and 0.030 octaves.
what_the_corner_table_is.why_it_matters: Two tables holding the same numbers and one table reached two ways return the same corners, so this is not separable here and is not claimed as one implementation. What it does rule out is two different tables: a filter given its own entries would have no reason to land inside a twentieth of an octave of the other's at all four.

alternatives.reading: The high pass runs at a different clock from the low pass, and the thirty-two kilohertz read off the low pass does not reach it.

separated_by.observable: The best run there is, and it is not enough. Sweeping the high pass to the top of its corner table rather than the bottom -- setting 127, where the table puts the corner near 8000 Hz and the band set still has room above it -- is where the two rates are furthest apart anywhere this filter can be put.

predicts.thirty-two kilohertz: The approach to the passband squeezed by the warp, 1.08 dB away at 25 Hz from where forty-four puts it.
predicts.forty-four point one: The same curve with that squeeze absent.

separated_by.sensitivity_here: 1.16 dB, which is what the run's own repeats spread at 25 Hz.
separated_by.why_not_separable: A first-order high pass has its zero at nothing and unity at half the rate, so below its corner the warp is invisible and above it the curve is flat whatever the clock is. There is no setting at which it is otherwise: the widest the two rates ever get on this filter is 1.08 dB, against a floor of 1.16 dB where it happens, a margin of 0.93 -- under one, so the run must not be queued. That is why the four settings on the record return the same median at every rate in the catalogue to a thousandth of a decibel: the reading cannot hear the question rather than the rates agreeing. What would answer it is not a band profile of this filter at all.

alternatives.reading: A conjugate pair sitting at a resonance so low that its corner looks like one pole's, rather than one pole.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The skirt, which a resonance does not touch. A pair runs at twelve decibels an octave however low its resonance is put, and the low pass runs at six over three octaves of skirt where the reading's own floor is under a fifth of a decibel. Scored through the same takes the pair's median is eleven times the winner's and its residual leans.

compared_against.generated_from: data/units/roland-sc8850-01/index.json, every efx-bands record filed under type 01 42 at address 40 03 04 at the twelfth-octave resolution

excluded.why: The same takes read at the third-octave set. A skirt read four times coarser is the same skirt with four times fewer points on it, and scoring both counts one measurement twice.
The same takes read at the third-octave set. A skirt read four times coarser is the same skirt with four times fewer points on it, and scoring both counts one measurement twice.

reproduces.how_the_model_is_read: Rendered through the very takes the record was read from and then measured on the same band set, with the chain's own silence added back where the model cuts below it. That last is not a correction fitted to anything: the unit filters its signal and then adds its own noise to what comes out, so a band it cuts forty decibels stops where its output stage is and goes no further, while a model rendered by filtering a take cuts the take's noise along with its signal and keeps going. The silence takes the run itself made are what is added back. Without it the winner was fifteen decibels out in the top band of the deepest setting and under a tenth everywhere shallow, which reads exactly like a model breaking down at one end of a byte and is not.

gross.why: median 0.08 dB against the 40.75 dB the low pass commands, and 0.07 against 21.43 on the high pass.

properties.why: The slope is a property of the pole count alone and the model returns it on both filters: six decibels an octave through the middle of the band, bending to ten near the top of the low pass and not at all on the high pass. And the corners the two filters return agree to within 0.064 octaves at every setting both were asked, which no candidate arranges -- each fits its own table.

power.how: contradicted on the low pass and outscored on the high
power.why: Two things separate and they separate differently. The order is contradicted: a second pole puts twelve decibels an octave where the unit has six, which is a slope the reading resolves several times over, and both second-order candidates come back leaning on both records. The rate is separated on the low pass alone, where the same one-pole section clocked at forty-four or forty-eight is four times the winner's median and leans, and on the high pass the three rates are indistinguishable -- which is carried as a standing alternative rather than as agreement.

breakdown.verdict: reproduces on the low pass, structure remains on the high

why.low: the signed median swings 0.425 dB across the settings and 0.9 dB across the readings within one, against the run's own floor of 2.09 dB
why.high: the signed median swings 0.025 dB across the settings and 4.685 dB across the readings within one, against the run's own floor of 2.09 dB

breakdown.read_as: The low pass is the record that separates the candidates and it is the only one of the five that does not lean on it. The high pass returns structure and the statistic is reporting scatter rather than a lean: below 56 Hz the run's own repeats of one setting disagree by up to 2.09 decibels against 0.04 above 100, and the winner's per-band median alternates sign there -- minus 0.97, minus 1.85, minus 0.43, plus 1.83, minus 2.26. The two-pole candidate on the same bands is negative at all of them and positive across the whole passband, which is a lean. The gate cannot tell those apart at the bottom of this band set and the verdict is left as it came back rather than being read into.

refuted_by: A setting of either filter whose skirt runs at a slope no whole number of poles gives, or a low pass whose skirt is still at six decibels an octave at the top of the band, which would put half the rate outside it. Or the same sweep on a corner byte of another type coming back at twelve, which would make the section this type's and not the part's.
what_this_does_not_settle: Whether every filter byte on this unit sits on the same section. Two addresses of one type were read and the class is written for the part, which is a reading of two and not of the archive. What argues for it beyond the era is that the equaliser's own shelves came back first-order on a separate comparison of thirty-one records, so the part is not spending pairs where it can spend poles.

What the fourth state of the type byte does. The page prints LPF+HPF and the run asked Off, LPF and HPF; whether that state is the two sections in series or a band pass written separately is not read here.

Where the corners are. That is the frequency class's, and the tables fitted here are a readout taken so that the shapes could be compared without handing one candidate another's corners -- not a second reading of a table already closed.
Whether the high pass shares the low pass's clock. Its own record cannot say, and the run that would is named in the alternatives.
